messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Alex is twenty-five and works in sales for a consumer electronics chain, a job that requires him to be on the phone with customers for most of the day. Three years ago, while visiting relatives in a region that had recently descended into armed conflict, he was caught in an outdoor marketplace when a mortar round struck several hundred feet away. The blast threw him to the ground; he remembers the screaming, the smell of dust and burnt metal, and the sight of a vendor’s stall collapsing onto people. He made it back to his family’s apartment, but for the next two weeks until he could evacuate, the shelling continued nightly. That period defined something inside him that has not let go.

Now, back in the United States and living with his girlfriend, Alex experiences strong negative emotions that surface unpredictably. In the middle of a routine sales pitch, a customer’s sharp tone can trigger a flash of anger that he has to stifle. At other times, guilt washes over him without warning—he thinks of the people who did not make it home, and he tells himself he should have done more to help. These feelings arrive and depart on their own schedule, and he has learned to just breathe through them until they pass.

Night vigilance is its own separate reality. As dusk settles, Alex’s body begins to brace. He checks the front door lock three times before bed, pulls the curtains shut so no light leaks in, and sleeps with a small flashlight on the nightstand. If his girlfriend shifts in her sleep or a car door slams outside, he is instantly awake, heart pounding, listening for the next sound. He has come to believe that darkness itself is dangerous, that the safety of daylight evaporates once the sun goes down. He avoids evening social plans whenever possible, and if he has to drive after dark, he takes the longest route to avoid quiet residential streets.

Concentration difficulty has become a practical obstacle at work. Alex used to be a top performer, but now he finds his attention slipping during phone calls. A customer will be describing a laptop model, and Alex’s mind will drift to something unrelated—a noise in the background, a memory fragment, a sudden urge to check the window. He has started using a notepad to jot down every detail the customer says, but even then, he sometimes has to ask them to repeat themselves twice. His manager has noticed the decline in his closing rates and has scheduled a performance review for next month.

None of these problems feel connected to each other in Alex’s mind. They are just separate burdens he carries. The negative emotions are a private storm that flares and fades; the night vigilance is a nightly ritual he cannot explain to his girlfriend; the concentration trouble is a work performance issue he hopes to fix with more coffee and longer hours. He does not see a thread running through them.

What finally brought Alex to seek help was his girlfriend’s gentle ultimatum. She told him she could not keep living with a partner who was present during the day but unreachable after dark, who flinched at her touch when she woke him from a nightmare. Alex agreed to come to therapy because he is afraid of losing her, and because he is even more afraid that the next time his supervisor reviews his numbers, he will be out of a job. What he hopes for, though he struggles to admit it, is to feel that the world is not still an active war zone—to sit through a quiet evening without scanning the windows, and to sleep through the night in the same bed as the woman he loves.
